title: Community support, C(E)TRs and avoiding admission
blurb: Use dynamic support registers and Care (Education) and Treatment Reviews to keep people well at home and challenge barriers to discharge.
question: Kieran, 24, is autistic with a learning disability. His placement is breaking down and his family say the GP has mentioned 'hospital'. He is on the local dynamic support register. What should the community learning disability nurse do to try to avoid an admission?

teach.body: After the abuse at Winterbourne View (2011), national policy set out to move people with a learning disability and autistic people out of long-stay mental health hospitals and to support them at home. The Building the Right Support action plan (2022) aimed to halve inpatient numbers by March 2024 compared with 2015; the target was missed (2,055 inpatients in February 2025, down 29%). In plain English: hospital is rarely the right place, so services must spot risk early and act in the community.
teach.cite: Building the Right Support action plan (DHSC, 2022); Commons Library SN07058

teach.body: Each local system keeps a dynamic support register of children, young people and adults with a learning disability or autistic people who are at risk of admission to a mental health hospital. Inclusion needs the person's informed consent, checked at least annually; if they lack capacity, consent comes from a lawful representative such as an attorney or deputy, or through a best interests decision if there is none. People and families can self-refer. Each person is risk-rated so the right support is offered early.
teach.cite: NHS England Dynamic support register and C(E)TR policy and guide (2023)

bands.label: Immediate risk; C(E)TR must take place

teach.caption: Red and amber ratings also prompt referral to the keyworker service for people aged 0–25.

teach.body: A Care and Treatment Review (CTR, adults) or Care, Education and Treatment Review (CETR, children and young people) is a person-centred review to make sure the person's care, education, treatment and support needs are met and that barriers to progress or discharge are challenged and overcome. It is not mandatory to be on the DSR to have one. The review does not decide admission or discharge; that remains a clinical (or court) decision.
teach.cite: NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy (2023), sections 9-13

head: Review
Adults (non-secure)
Children and young people
teach.caption: After a community review, a further review follows 6 weeks after admission. Secure adult pathways repeat every 12 months.
An expert by experience is someone with lived experience or a family member of someone with lived experience.

teach.h: The six key lines of enquiry
head: Question asked from the person's view
Focus
rows: What is my current care like?
What is my daily life like?
Are my physical health needs being met?
Is there a plan in place for my future?
Do I need to be in hospital?
teach.caption: Reviewers record quotes from the person and family under each line of enquiry.

teach.body: Kieran, 24, is on the DSR and his placement is breaking down. The nurse raises his rating from amber to red with the multi-agency DSR meeting, which means a community CTR must take place. She makes sure Kieran has an advocate and that his family's views are heard. The CTR asks what support at home could prevent admission: crisis outreach, an updated behaviour support plan, a review of his medication and a short-term increase in staffing. Its recommendations are tracked.

teach.text: Three traps: a C(E)TR cannot block an urgent admission that a clinician judges necessary, but a post-admission review must still follow; it does not itself decide admission or discharge; and the Mental Health Act 2025 will put these reviews and registers on a statutory footing for detained patients, but those provisions are not yet in force.

items: DSR: people at risk of mental health admission; consent needed; RAG rated; self-referral possible.
Red rating: a community C(E)TR must take place.
No community review: post-admission review within 28 days (adults) or 14 days (children).
Panel: commissioner (chair), independent clinical expert, expert by experience.
C(E)TRs challenge barriers; clinicians still decide admission and discharge.

summary: You can now use the dynamic support register and risk ratings to spot people at risk early, explain when community and post-admission C(E)TRs happen and who sits on the panel, and use the review to challenge barriers to staying at home or getting home.

A.q: What is the purpose of a dynamic support register?
options: To list everyone with a learning disability in a GP practice
To identify people at risk of admission to a mental health hospital
To record people detained under the Mental Health Act
To list people waiting for a learning disability diagnosis
A.why: The DSR identifies children, young people and adults with a learning disability or autistic people who are at risk of admission to a mental health hospital, so support can be offered early.

whyNot.0: That describes the GP learning disability register.
whyNot.2: Detained patients are recorded through MHA processes; the DSR focuses on risk.
whyNot.3: The DSR is not a diagnostic waiting list.

A.q: An adult with a learning disability is admitted to a mental health hospital without a community CTR. Within what timescale must a post-admission CTR take place?
A.why: NHS England policy: if no community CTR was held, a post-admission CTR must take place within 28 days (20 working days) for adults.

whyNot.0: Seven days is not a timescale in the policy.
whyNot.1: Fourteen days applies to children and young people.
whyNot.3: Six weeks is the follow-up after a community CTR, not the post-admission maximum.

A.q: Which member must be included on every C(E)TR panel alongside the chair and an independent clinical expert?
A.why: The panel must include the responsible commissioner as chair, an independent clinical expert and an independent expert by experience.

whyNot.0: The GP may contribute but is not a required panel member.
whyNot.1: The clinical expert role is independent and need not be a psychiatrist.

B.q: Freya, 15, is autistic and is admitted to a children's mental health unit in a crisis without a community CETR. When must her CETR take place?
B.why: For children and young people, a post-admission CETR must take place within 14 days (10 working days) if no community CETR was held.

whyNot.2: Six weeks is the follow-up after a community review.
whyNot.3: Three months is the repeat interval for children.

B.q: On the DSR, Joel, 30, is rated red. What does the policy require?
options: A referral to the police liaison team
A community C(E)TR to take place
A review at the next annual health check
B.why: Red means an immediate risk of admission to a mental health hospital, and the policy's linked process is that a C(E)TR must take place to look for community alternatives.

whyNot.0: Police liaison is not the required response to a red rating.
whyNot.1: The aim is to avoid unnecessary admission; the C(E)TR looks for community alternatives.
whyNot.3: Waiting for an annual check is far too slow for immediate risk.

B.q: A psychiatrist judges that Leo, 28, who has a learning disability, needs urgent admission because of serious risk. His community CTR cannot be arranged in time. What does the policy say?
options: The admission must wait until the CTR is held
The CTR panel decides whether he is admitted
Leo must be removed from the DSR on admission
Admission proceeds; a post-admission CTR follows
B.why: A C(E)TR must not delay a clinically necessary urgent admission, and a post-admission review must still be held within the timescales.

whyNot.0: The policy says reviews should not delay or obstruct urgent admission.
whyNot.1: The review does not decide admission; clinicians do.
whyNot.2: He is rated blue as an inpatient, not removed.

C.q: Kieran, 24, is autistic with a learning disability. He is on the DSR, rated amber. His placement is now breaking down and his GP mentions hospital. What should the community nurse do first?
options: Refer Kieran directly to an inpatient assessment unit
Raise his risk rating and request a community CTR
Wait for the placement to end before taking action
Ask the GP to start an antipsychotic to stabilise him
C.why: Escalating risk calls for a review of his DSR rating and a community CTR, which looks for alternatives to admission and challenges barriers.

whyNot.0: Referral for admission skips the review designed to avoid it.
whyNot.2: Waiting loses the chance for early intervention.
whyNot.3: NICE NG11 1.8.2 considers antipsychotics only after other interventions or treatment of coexisting problems have failed, or when risk is very severe, and then only alongside psychological support; this skips the review.

C.q: Amina, 22, has a learning disability and has been an inpatient for 8 months. Her CTR finds she is clinically ready for discharge but no suitable home has been found. What is the main purpose of the CTR here?
options: To decide to discharge her to any available bed
To approve a further 12 months in hospital
To challenge barriers to discharge and set actions
To transfer her to a secure service for safety
C.why: C(E)TRs ensure needs are met and challenge barriers to progress or discharge, with recommendations and actions tracked by commissioners.

whyNot.0: The review does not make the discharge decision, and any bed is not a plan.
whyNot.1: Approving a long stay is not the review's purpose.
whyNot.3: Moving to a more restrictive setting is not indicated when she is ready for discharge.

C.q: Ben, 35, has a learning disability and capacity to decide about sharing his information. He declines to be added to the dynamic support register. What should happen?
options: Respect his decision; his care must not be affected
Add him to the register because he is at high risk
Ask his mother to consent to his inclusion instead
Discharge him from the community team caseload
C.why: Inclusion on the DSR requires informed consent. Withholding consent must not affect current care, and people not on the DSR can still have a C(E)TR.

whyNot.1: Adding a capacitous adult without consent breaches the policy.
whyNot.2: A relative cannot consent for a capacitous adult.
whyNot.3: Declining the register must not affect his care.

reteach.title: Spot early, review, keep home
reteach.question: If you could see a crisis coming months away, what would you put in place?

blocks.body: The DSR is the local radar of people at risk of admission. The RAG rating shows how close the risk is. When it turns red, a community C(E)TR brings an independent clinician and an expert by experience round the table to find a way to keep the person safe at home. If admission happens anyway, a review follows quickly to plan the way out.

blocks.text: 28 days is the adult deadline; 14 days is for children and young people.

explain.body: A register of people at risk of mental health admission, with consent, risk rated and regularly reviewed by a multi-agency group.

test.q: How often should consent for inclusion on the DSR be checked as a minimum?
test.why: The policy says consent should be checked at least annually and the dates recorded.

whyNot.0: Monthly is more often than the stated minimum.
whyNot.1: Six-monthly is not the stated minimum.

explain.body: Red: immediate risk; amber: risk without urgent help; green: risks managed; blue: currently an inpatient.

test.q: Which DSR rating identifies people who are currently inpatients?
test.why: A separate blue rating identifies people currently in inpatient services.

whyNot.0: Red is immediate risk in the community.
whyNot.1: Amber is risk without urgent intervention.

explain.body: Community C(E)TR before admission. If none: adults within 28 days, children within 14 days. Repeat: adults 6-monthly (non-secure), children 3-monthly.

test.q: How often should repeat CETRs take place for a young person in a non-secure mental health hospital?
test.why: For children and young people, repeat CETRs take place at least every 3 months.

whyNot.0: Monthly is not the policy minimum.
whyNot.2: Six months applies to adults in non-secure services.
whyNot.3: Twelve months applies to adults in secure services.

explain.h: What the review does and does not do
explain.body: It reviews care and challenges barriers. It does not decide admission or discharge, and it must not delay a necessary urgent admission.

test.q: Who decides whether a person is admitted to a mental health hospital?
test.why: Admission and discharge remain the responsibility of clinicians (or courts under Part 3 of the MHA); the C(E)TR makes recommendations.

whyNot.0: The chair leads the review but does not decide admission.
whyNot.1: The expert by experience contributes to recommendations.
whyNot.2: Oversight panels review progress, not admission decisions.
